title: North Texas Is Getting Up to 2 Inches of Rain in One Weekend — Why That's a Bigger Risk to Balcony Pots Than the Cooldown Behind It
intro: Dallas-Fort Worth is in the middle of a fast pattern flip this weekend. The Dallas Morning News is reporting storms could bring up to 2 inches of rain into Sunday, WFAA has been tracking the same system under the headline "Dallas, Texas freeze forecast: Latest DFW weather update," and a local report out Friday (via Rolling Out) described a strong storm system rolling into North Texas off the back of an unusually warm stretch of November weather — Fox4's own framing of the pattern was blunt: "record-warm November gives way to hard freeze, more rain." NWS Fort Worth's forecast has rain chances climbing to roughly 69% by midnight Saturday and near 97% by early Sunday morning, with most of the rain falling before late Sunday morning, and highs crashing to only the low 50s Sunday and near 57 Monday behind it. For apartment and balcony growers across DFW, the cooldown itself is mild — the low 50s won't hurt the vast majority of potted plants. The part worth actually paying attention to is the 1-2 inches of rain landing in a single overnight window on containers that have spent weeks in mild, dry fall weather.

sections.heading: Why a fast 1-2 inch dump hits a pot harder than it hits a garden bed
sections.body: In-ground soil has somewhere for a sudden downpour to go — it percolates sideways and down into the surrounding earth. A container doesn't have that luxury: water can only leave through the drainage holes in the bottom, and if those holes are sitting in a saucer, cachepot, or a self-watering reservoir that's already full, the water has nowhere to go at all. A pot that gets 1-2 inches of rain in a few hours ends up sitting in standing water at exactly the root zone for as long as that saucer stays full, which after an overnight storm can mean most of Sunday. That's a materially different stress than the same rain falling on a garden bed, and it's worse than usual right now specifically because DFW containers have been through a dry, mild stretch — potting mix that's gone a while between waterings doesn't handle a sudden saturation event as gracefully as mix that's been getting regular moisture, and roots that aren't used to sitting wet are the ones most likely to start rotting if the water doesn't drain promptly once the storm passes.

sections.heading: The one-step fix: get the pot off the saucer, not just the water out of it
sections.body: The practical move isn't complicated, but it only works if you do it before the rain arrives, not after: raise pots up off their saucers or off the balcony floor so water has somewhere to go besides pooling under the drainage holes. Flat-bottomed pots sitting directly on a saucer or a solid balcony floor can effectively seal their own drainage holes once water backs up around them. A set of simple pot feet — small risers that lift the base of the container a half-inch or so — keeps that gap open so runoff actually drains away instead of wicking straight back up into the root ball. Achla Designs' pot feet are a widely available option sized for standard container gardening rather than oversized patio urns, and they're reusable season to season, so this isn't a one-weekend purchase — it's useful for every heavy-rain event the rest of fall and winter brings.

sections.heading: Don't forget the wind side of a storm system, not just the rain side
sections.body: A system big enough to bring 1-2 inches of rain and thunderstorms to North Texas this weekend is also a system big enough to bring gusty outflow winds ahead of and during the rain, and a top-heavy potted plant — a tall tomato or pepper still in its cage, a trellised vine, a tropical with a lot of leaf surface up high — is far easier to knock over on a balcony than the same plant would be in a garden bed with roots anchored into the ground. If you've got anything tall or top-heavy out there, it's worth staking or tying it to the railing before Saturday night rather than finding it tipped over, soil spilled and roots exposed, Sunday morning. A simple set of adjustable garden stakes with clips can brace a container plant to a railing or to its own pot rim in a few minutes, and they come down easily once the system clears.

conclusion: None of this requires overreacting to a system that, temperature-wise, is genuinely mild — the low 50s behind this front isn't a freeze and won't stress the great majority of container plants. The actual to-do list is narrower and more immediate: get pots up off saucers or solid flooring before the rain starts so Sunday's 1-2 inches has somewhere to drain instead of somewhere to pool, and tie down or stake anything tall and top-heavy against the wind that comes with the same storm system. Once the rain clears Sunday morning, resist the urge to water again for several days — a dump like this is enough moisture to carry most containers through the following week even with cooler, drier air settling in behind it.
